imo-2005-01.title: Vectors / complex numbers
imo-2005-01.body:
Let $s$ be the common side length. Place the triangle in the complex plane with $B\to C$ the positive real direction and $A$ above $BC$, so $B\to C\to A$ is counterclockwise. With $\omega=e^{2\pi i/3}$, the unit vectors in the directions $B\to C$, $C\to A$, $A\to B$ are $1,\omega,\omega^2$.

**Orientation of the hexagon.** Going around the convex hexagon $A_1A_2B_1B_2C_1C_2$ we pass from $BC$ to $CA$ to $AB$, so the hexagon is traversed counterclockwise, $A_2$ is nearer $C$ than $A_1$, and so on. Hence, as complex numbers,
$$A_2-A_1=s,\qquad B_2-B_1=s\omega,\qquad C_2-C_1=s\omega^2 .$$
Write $p=B_1-A_2$, $q=C_1-B_2$, $r=A_1-C_2$; these have modulus $s$. The six side vectors sum to $0$ and $s(1+\omega+\omega^2)=0$, so $p+q+r=0$.

**Three equal-length vectors with zero sum.** Put $t=q/p$, $|t|=1$. From $|p+q|=|r|=|p|$ we get $|1+t|=1$; together with $|t|=1$ this gives $t=\omega$ or $t=\omega^2$ (the two intersection points of the unit circles centred at $0$ and $-1$).

**Convexity rules out $t=\omega^2$.** In a convex polygon traversed counterclockwise each side vector is obtained from the previous one by a counterclockwise turn through an angle strictly between $0^\circ$ and $180^\circ$. Let $p=se^{i\alpha}$. The turn from $s$ (argument $0^\circ$) to $p$ gives $0<\alpha<180^\circ$. If $q=p\omega^2$ (argument $\alpha+240^\circ$), the turn from $q$ to $C_2-C_1=s\omega^2$ (argument $240^\circ$) is $-\alpha \pmod{360^\circ}$, i.e. $360^\circ-\alpha>180^\circ$ — impossible. So $q=p\omega$ and $r=-p-q=p\omega^2$.

**$A_1B_1C_1$ is equilateral.** Now
$$B_1-A_1=s+p,\qquad C_1-B_1=s\omega+q=\omega(s+p),\qquad A_1-C_1=s\omega^2+r=\omega^2(s+p),$$
so the three sides of triangle $A_1B_1C_1$ have the same length $|s+p|$.

**Conclusion.** $B_2$ satisfies $B_2B_1=B_2C_1=s$ (sides of the hexagon), and $A_1B_1=A_1C_1$. So both $A_1$ and $B_2$ lie on the perpendicular bisector of $B_1C_1$, and since $A_1\ne B_2$ the line $A_1B_2$ *is* this perpendicular bisector. In the same way $B_1C_2$ is the perpendicular bisector of $C_1A_1$ and $C_1A_2$ is the perpendicular bisector of $A_1B_1$. The three perpendicular bisectors of a triangle meet at its circumcentre, so the three lines are concurrent. ∎

imo-2005-02.title: Growing blocks of consecutive integers
imo-2005-02.body:
**Step 1: distinct terms, and $|a_i-a_j|<j$ for $i<j$.** If $a_i=a_j$ with $i<j$, take $n=j$: then $a_i\equiv a_j\pmod j$, contradicting that $a_1,\dots,a_j$ leave different remainders mod $j$. So all terms are distinct. If $i<j$ and $n:=|a_i-a_j|\ge j$, then $i<j\le n$ and $a_i\equiv a_j\pmod n$, again contradicting the hypothesis for this $n$. Hence $|a_i-a_j|\le j-1$.

**Step 2: for every $n$, $\{a_1,\dots,a_n\}=\{k+1,k+2,\dots,k+n\}$ for some integer $k$.** Induction on $n$; $n=1$ is trivial. Suppose $\{a_1,\dots,a_n\}=\{k+1,\dots,k+n\}$. These $n$ consecutive integers occupy every residue class mod $n+1$ except the class of $k\equiv k+n+1$. Since $a_1,\dots,a_{n+1}$ have distinct residues mod $n+1$, we get $a_{n+1}\equiv k\pmod{n+1}$. By Step 1 (with $j=n+1$), $a_{n+1}$ differs from both $k+1$ and $k+n$ by at most $n$, so $k\le a_{n+1}\le k+n+1$. The only numbers in $[k,k+n+1]$ congruent to $k$ mod $n+1$ are $k$ and $k+n+1$, so $\{a_1,\dots,a_{n+1}\}$ is $\{k,\dots,k+n\}$ or $\{k+1,\dots,k+n+1\}$ — again consecutive.

**Step 3: every integer appears.** The terms are distinct integers, and there are infinitely many positive and infinitely many negative ones, so the sequence is unbounded above and below. Given any integer $m$, choose $i$ with $a_i>m$ and $j$ with $a_j<m$, and let $n=\max(i,j)$. By Step 2, $\{a_1,\dots,a_n\}$ is a set of consecutive integers containing $a_j<m<a_i$, hence it contains $m$.

Together with distinctness, every integer occurs exactly once. ∎

imo-2005-03.title: Compare each term with a common denominator
imo-2005-03.body:
Let $S=x^2+y^2+z^2$.

**Claim.** $\dfrac{x^5-x^2}{x^5+y^2+z^2}\ge \dfrac{x^5-x^2}{x^3S}=\dfrac{x^2-\frac1x}{S}$.

Indeed,
$$\frac{x^5-x^2}{x^5+y^2+z^2}-\frac{x^5-x^2}{x^3S}=\frac{(x^5-x^2)\,\bigl(x^3S-x^5-y^2-z^2\bigr)}{x^3S\,(x^5+y^2+z^2)} .$$
Here $x^3S-x^5-y^2-z^2=x^3y^2+x^3z^2-y^2-z^2=(x^3-1)(y^2+z^2)$ and $x^5-x^2=x^2(x^3-1)$, so the numerator equals $x^2(x^3-1)^2(y^2+z^2)\ge 0$, and the denominator is positive.

**Summing.** Adding the claim and its two cyclic versions,
$$\sum_{\text{cyc}}\frac{x^5-x^2}{x^5+y^2+z^2}\ \ge\ \frac{x^2+y^2+z^2-\left(\frac1x+\frac1y+\frac1z\right)}{S}.$$
Since $xyz\ge 1$ we have $\frac1x\le \frac{xyz}{x}=yz$, and similarly $\frac1y\le zx$, $\frac1z\le xy$. Hence
$$\frac1x+\frac1y+\frac1z\le xy+yz+zx\le x^2+y^2+z^2,$$
the last step being $\tfrac12\left[(x-y)^2+(y-z)^2+(z-x)^2\right]\ge 0$. So the right-hand side above is $\ge 0$. ∎

imo-2005-03.title: Cauchy–Schwarz
imo-2005-03.body:
Since $\dfrac{x^5-x^2}{x^5+y^2+z^2}=1-\dfrac{S}{x^5+y^2+z^2}$ with $S=x^2+y^2+z^2$, the inequality is equivalent to
$$\sum_{\text{cyc}}\frac{1}{x^5+y^2+z^2}\le\frac{3}{S}.$$
By Cauchy–Schwarz, $(x^5+y^2+z^2)\left(\frac1x+y^2+z^2\right)\ge (x^2+y^2+z^2)^2=S^2$, so
$$\frac{1}{x^5+y^2+z^2}\le\frac{\frac1x+y^2+z^2}{S^2}.$$
Summing cyclically, $\displaystyle\sum\frac{1}{x^5+y^2+z^2}\le\frac{\frac1x+\frac1y+\frac1z+2S}{S^2}$. As in the first solution, $\frac1x+\frac1y+\frac1z\le xy+yz+zx\le S$, so the sum is at most $\frac{3S}{S^2}=\frac3S$. ∎

imo-2005-04.title: Every prime divides some term
imo-2005-04.body:
The number $1$ is relatively prime to everything. We show that every prime $p$ divides some $a_n$; then any positive integer $m>1$ (which has a prime factor $p$) shares the factor $p$ with some term.

- $p=2$ and $p=3$: $a_2=4+9+36-1=48=2^4\cdot 3$.
- $p\ge 5$: then $p\nmid 6$, and by Fermat's little theorem $2^{p-1}\equiv 3^{p-1}\equiv 6^{p-1}\equiv 1\pmod p$. Hence
$$6\,a_{p-2}=3\cdot 2^{p-1}+2\cdot 3^{p-1}+6^{p-1}-6\equiv 3+2+1-6=0\pmod p .$$
Since $\gcd(6,p)=1$, $p\mid a_{p-2}$ (and $p-2\ge 3$ is a valid index).

So the only positive integer coprime to all terms is $1$.

**Answer: 1**

imo-2005-05.title: Centre of rotation (Miquel point)
imo-2005-05.body:
We use directed angles $\measuredangle(\ell,m)$ between lines, taken mod $180^\circ$; four points $W,X,Y,Z$ are concyclic iff $\measuredangle(YW,YX)=\measuredangle(ZW,ZX)$.

**The rotation.** Since $DA=BC$ and the segments are not parallel, there is a rotation $\rho$ with centre $M$ such that $\rho(D)=B$ and $\rho(A)=C$ (a translation is excluded because the vectors $\overrightarrow{DA}$ and $\overrightarrow{BC}$ are not equal). $\rho$ maps segment $DA$ onto segment $BC$ preserving distances, so the point $F$ of $DA$ with $DF=t$ goes to the point of $BC$ at distance $t$ from $B$, i.e. $\rho(F)=E$. The point $M$ depends only on $ABCD$.

$M\ne P$: otherwise $PD=PB$ and $PA=PC$, so the diagonals bisect each other, $ABCD$ is a parallelogram and $BC\parallel DA$ — contradiction.

**Lemma.** If a rotation (or spiral similarity) with centre $M$ maps $X\mapsto X'$ and $Y\mapsto Y'$, and the lines $XX'$ and $YY'$ meet at $T$, then $M,T,X,Y$ are concyclic.

*Proof.* Triangles $MXX'$ and $MYY'$ are directly similar (both are isosceles with apex angle the rotation angle, resp. have the same angle and ratio). Hence $\measuredangle(XX',XM)=\measuredangle(YY',YM)$, i.e. $\measuredangle(XT,XM)=\measuredangle(YT,YM)$, which means $M,T,X,Y$ are concyclic. $\square$

**Applying the lemma.**
- With $X=D$, $Y=A$ ($X'=B$, $Y'=C$): $XX'\cap YY'=BD\cap AC=P$, so $M,P,D,A$ are concyclic.
- With $X=D$, $Y=F$ ($X'=B$, $Y'=E$): $XX'\cap YY'=BD\cap EF=Q$, so $M,Q,D,F$ are concyclic.

**$M$ lies on $(PQR)$.** The points $Q,R,F$ lie on line $EF$; $P,R,A$ lie on line $AC$; $D,F,A$ lie on line $DA$. Therefore
$$\measuredangle(QM,QR)=\measuredangle(QM,QF)=\measuredangle(DM,DF)=\measuredangle(DM,DA)=\measuredangle(PM,PA)=\measuredangle(PM,PR),$$
using the circle $MQDF$ for the second equality and the circle $MPDA$ for the fourth. Hence $M,P,Q,R$ are concyclic.

So every circumcircle $(PQR)$ passes through the fixed point $M\ne P$. ∎

imo-2005-06.title: Double counting and a congruence mod 3
imo-2005-06.body:
Let $n$ be the number of contestants and, for problems $i\ne j$, let $p_{ij}$ be the number of contestants who solved both $i$ and $j$. Since $p_{ij}>\frac25n$ and $5p_{ij}$ is an integer, $5p_{ij}\ge 2n+1$.

**Double counting.** A contestant who solved $m$ problems solved $\binom m2$ pairs, so
$$\sum_{i<j}p_{ij}=\sum_{\text{contestants}}\binom{m}{2}.$$
The left side is at least $15\cdot\frac{2n+1}{5}=6n+3$.

Suppose, for contradiction, that at most one contestant solved exactly $5$ problems. Nobody solved $6$, so every other contestant contributes at most $\binom42=6$.
- If nobody solved $5$, the right side is at most $6n<6n+3$. Impossible.
- So exactly one contestant (call him $Z$) solved $5$ problems, contributing $10$. If some other contestant solved at most $3$ problems, the sum is at most $10+6(n-2)+3=6n+1$. Impossible. So **every other contestant solved exactly $4$ problems**, and the sum equals $10+6(n-1)=6n+4$.

**The pair counts.** Now $\sum p_{ij}=6n+4$ with each $p_{ij}\ge\frac{2n+1}5$. If $5\nmid 2n+1$, then $5p_{ij}\ge 2n+2$ for every pair and the sum would be at least $3(2n+2)=6n+6$. So $k:=\frac{2n+1}5$ is an integer and $\sum p_{ij}=15k+1$ with all $p_{ij}\ge k$: **fourteen of the $p_{ij}$ equal $k$ and one equals $k+1$.**

**A congruence.** Number the problems so that $Z$ solved $1,\dots,5$ and not $6$. For a problem $j$ let $x_j$ be the number of contestants who solved $j$, and look at $\sigma_j=\sum_{i\ne j}p_{ij}$, which counts pairs (contestant who solved $j$, another problem he solved).
- For $j=6$: every solver of problem $6$ solved exactly $4$ problems, so $\sigma_6=3x_6\equiv 0\pmod 3$.
- For $j\in\{1,\dots,5\}$: $Z$ contributes $4$ and every other solver contributes $3$, so $\sigma_j=3(x_j-1)+4\equiv 1\pmod 3$.

Each $\sigma_j$ is a sum of five of the $p$'s, so $\sigma_j=5k+1$ if the exceptional pair contains $j$ and $\sigma_j=5k$ otherwise.
- If the exceptional pair contains problem $6$, it is $\{6,i\}$ for one $i\le5$. Then $\sigma_6=5k+1\equiv 0$, while for a problem $j\le 5$, $j\ne i$, $\sigma_j=5k\equiv 1\pmod 3$. These give $5k\equiv 2$ and $5k\equiv 1\pmod 3$, a contradiction.
- If it does not contain $6$, then $\sigma_6=5k\equiv 0$, and for one of the three problems $j\le5$ outside the exceptional pair, $\sigma_j=5k\equiv1\pmod 3$ — again a contradiction.

Hence at least two contestants solved exactly $5$ problems. ∎
